planting.note: Plant container-grown cactus in spring in lean, rocky to gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; green-flowered hedgehog cactus is exceptionally cold-hardy for a cactus and tolerates winter snow cover better than many desert species.

directions: Plant container-grown cactus in spring in lean, rocky to gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; green-flowered hedgehog cactus is exceptionally cold-hardy for a cactus and tolerates winter snow cover better than many desert species. Small, cylindrical, densely spined stems bear an unusual, subtly fragrant, yellow-green flower in spring, a muted color rare among the typically vivid pink, red, and magenta blooms of most hedgehog cacti, opening low to the ground on a compact plant well suited to a rock garden. Native to short-grass prairie and rocky plains from the Dakotas to Texas, it is remarkably cold-hardy, tolerating winter temperatures well below zero and surviving under snow cover that would kill most other cacti, making it a genuine option for a cold-climate xeriscape or rock garden. Water only occasionally once established, provide sharp drainage above all else, and avoid winter wet, which is more damaging than cold to this hardy species.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Plant container-grown cactus in spring in lean, rocky to gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Engelmann's hedgehog cactus needs sharp drainage and thrives in desert heat once established.

directions: Plant container-grown cactus in spring in lean, rocky to gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Engelmann's hedgehog cactus needs sharp drainage and thrives in desert heat once established. Clustering, cylindrical stems densely armed with long, colorful spines in shades of tan, gray, and reddish-brown eventually form substantial multi-stemmed mounds, bursting into a spectacular flush of large, vivid magenta-pink flowers each spring that rank among the showiest blooms of any Southwest desert cactus. Native to the Mojave and Sonoran Deserts, it is a familiar sight in rocky washes and desert flats across the Southwest, forming impressive colonies over many decades of slow growth. Water only occasionally once established, provide full sun and sharp drainage, and be patient, since this long-lived species grows slowly but rewards years of minimal care with an increasingly spectacular spring flower display.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; thimble cactus offsets prolifically and is one of the easiest, fastest-clustering small cacti to grow.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; thimble cactus offsets prolifically and is one of the easiest, fastest-clustering small cacti to grow. Small, cylindrical, pale green stems covered in fine white spines detach easily and root readily wherever they fall, causing the plant to spread and cluster with unusual speed compared to most mammillaria species, quickly filling a dish garden or small pot with dozens of small offsets. Small, pale yellow-white flowers ring the crown of mature stems in spring, though the plant is grown chiefly for its easy, fast-multiplying habit rather than a dramatic bloom display. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright light for compact growth, and simply replant any detached offset segments to propagate more plants.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Rose Pincushion Cactus needs excellent drainage and rots quickly if left in wet soil.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Rose Pincushion Cactus needs excellent drainage and rots quickly if left in wet soil. Densely packed, hooked golden-brown spines cover a cylindrical, slowly clustering stem topped each spring with a striking ring of vivid rose-pink to magenta flowers that circle the crown just below the growing point, one of the more reliably free-flowering mammillaria species for a sunny windowsill collection. Native to central Mexico, it slowly forms small clusters of stems over years of growth, eventually developing into an attractive mounded specimen without the aggressive, rapid offsetting of faster-clustering mammillaria species. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright direct light for the best spine color and most reliable flowering, and protect from frost.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Mother-of-Hundreds cactus clusters vigorously into a large mound and needs a spacious pot to accommodate its spread.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Mother-of-Hundreds cactus clusters vigorously into a large mound and needs a spacious pot to accommodate its spread. Flattened, densely clustering stems armed with stout white to brownish spines multiply rapidly from a single plant into a wide, dense mound of dozens of individual heads, living up to its common name within just a few years of vigorous offsetting, topped each spring by a ring of small, bright pink-purple flowers. Native to central Mexico, it is one of the fastest-clustering and most reliably free-flowering mammillaria species, making an impressive large specimen for a sunny patio or greenhouse given enough years and pot space to spread. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright direct light, and repot into a wider container as the clustering mound grows to accommodate its spread.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Plant container-grown cactus in spring in lean, gravelly to rocky, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; California barrel cactus needs sharp drainage and full desert sun, and rots quickly in wet or heavy soil.

directions: Plant container-grown cactus in spring in lean, gravelly to rocky, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; California barrel cactus needs sharp drainage and full desert sun, and rots quickly in wet or heavy soil. Thick, ribbed, cylindrical stems densely armed with long, curved, colorful spines ranging from yellow to red slowly grow into an iconic barrel shape over many decades, topped in summer with a ring of yellow to orange flowers followed by small yellow fruit, a familiar and long-lived architectural presence across the Mojave and Sonoran Deserts. Extremely slow-growing and long-lived, individual plants can live over a century in the wild, making a mature specimen a significant, irreplaceable landscape investment best sourced from nursery-propagated stock rather than wild-collected plants, which are protected in many areas. Water only occasionally once established, provide maximum sun and heat, and never allow the base to sit in standing water, which quickly causes fatal rot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Plant container-grown cactus in spring in lean, gravelly to rocky, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; spiny star cactus needs sharp drainage and is best grown in a raised bed or rock garden in wetter climates.

directions: Plant container-grown cactus in spring in lean, gravelly to rocky, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; spiny star cactus needs sharp drainage and is best grown in a raised bed or rock garden in wetter climates. Small, cylindrical, densely spined stems slowly cluster into small groups, producing vivid magenta-pink, star-shaped flowers in spring that open wide in full sun and rank among the more striking blooms of the smaller Chihuahuan Desert cacti. Native to limestone hills and desert scrub of west Texas and northern Mexico, it thrives on poor, rocky, alkaline soil and full desert sun, making it a good choice for a small-scale rock garden or trough planting alongside other miniature desert cacti and succulents. Water only occasionally once established, provide sharp drainage above all else, and protect from prolonged winter wet, which is more damaging than cold.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in extremely fast-draining, mineral cactus mix; Turbinicarpus is a slow-growing miniature that needs sharp drainage and careful, infrequent watering.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in extremely fast-draining, mineral cactus mix; Turbinicarpus is a slow-growing miniature that needs sharp drainage and careful, infrequent watering. A tiny, solitary or sparsely clustering globular cactus covered in fine, twisted, papery-textured spines produces surprisingly large, delicate pink flowers relative to its diminutive body size, a favorite among miniature cactus collectors for its slow, compact growth and reliable, showy blooms even at a very small size. Native to limestone desert habitats in northeastern Mexico, it is a slow-growing species that rewards patient, careful cultivation with a long-lived, collectible specimen well suited to a windowsill dish garden of miniature cacti. Water sparingly and infrequently, provide maximum bright light, and use an especially mineral, fast-draining mix, since this species is particularly prone to rot from overwatering.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference
